subject: physics
question_text: What is centripetal acceleration? Write its expression and its direction.

verification.note: PREDICTED — Session 89 enumeration sweep (archetype × object grid over the NCERT chapter): this question has not appeared in any paper or source book we hold, but the chapter contains it and the 2-mark/4-mark format admits it. Authored as a lean card; promote to a full card when a paper season or a Telangana IPE teacher validates the cell. Split invented, as everywhere.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The idea
lines: In uniform circular motion the speed stays
the same, but the direction of the velocity
keeps turning. That change of direction is
steps.margin_note: First mark. The change of direction is the definition — say it in words before any formula.
steps.why: Acceleration means a change of VELOCITY, and a velocity changes when its direction changes even if its size never does.
common_mistakes: Saying there is no acceleration because the speed is constant.

recall.must_convey: That the direction of velocity keeps changing in circular motion, and that change is the centripetal acceleration.

steps.memory_tip: Constant SPEED is not constant VELOCITY. A turning direction is already an acceleration.

steps.label: The expression
lines: It points along the radius, towards the
centre of the circle. That is why it is
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The formula alone will not earn it — the words "towards the centre" must appear.
steps.why: The direction is the part students drop, and it is the part that makes the motion circular rather than straight.
common_mistakes: Writing the direction as along the velocity, or outward instead of inward.

recall.must_convey: That a is v squared by r, equal to omega squared r, directed towards the centre.

steps.memory_tip: v²/r and ω²r are the same number, since v = ωr. Use whichever the question gives.

insider_note: Two marks: what it is, then a = v²/r. The direction towards the centre is part of the second mark, so write it.
